definition: Appetitive conditioning is learning in which a stimulus becomes associated with a reward or other attractive outcome, so it tends to be approached or chosen. In the packet, it is contrasted with aversion conditioning and described as part of differential training in which the rewarded stimulus is learned as the positive target.

reasons: The packet does not define appetitive conditioning as learning a stimulus becomes associated with reward or an attractive outcome, nor that it tends to be approached or chosen; those are unsupported generalizations.

The packet supports appetitive conditioning only as something used alongside aversion conditioning in a differential conditioning procedure, not as a stated definition or as a ‘positive target’ in the way the definition phrases it.

The packet does not explicitly state that appetitive conditioning is learning that “tends to be approached.” It only describes that CS+ (rewarded) and CS− (non-rewarded) are learned and that “choice following conditioning with a CS+ and a CS− results” from the interaction of excitatory/inhibitory traces.

While the packet supports that appetitive conditioning is used alongside aversion conditioning within a differential conditioning procedure and that the rewarded target (CS+) functions as the positive/excitatory target, the specific phrasing about appetitive conditioning causing approach is not directly supported by the provided text.
